content: In his book The Psychic Mafia, Keene recounts the story of a psychic medium named Raoul. Despite Raoul openly admitting that he was a fraud, some individuals continued to believe in his authenticity. This demonstrates that no amount of logical reasoning can dismantle a belief that is consciously built upon a falsehood. According to The Skeptic's Dictionary, another example of this phenomenon occurred in 1988. At the request of an Australian news program, James Randi coached stage performer José Alvarez to impersonate a channeler of a 2,000-year-old spirit named Carlos. Even after it was publicly revealed that Carlos was a fictional character created by Randi and Alvarez, many people persisted in their belief that Carlos was real. Randi remarked that no amount of evidence, regardless of its quality or quantity, could ever persuade a true believer to think otherwise. In the context of 419 scams, also known as advance fee fraud, perpetrators deceive victims into providing their bank details under the pretense of facilitating a large deposit. In reality, the goal is to drain the victim's account. Anti-419 activists use the term true believers to describe individuals who, despite evidence to the contrary, continue to trust in the supposed good intentions of the fraudsters.
